reviews.review: You'd better like reading. I like books, but I don't enjoy reading in games too much. Wasn't helped in this game that the important pieces of text are highlighted so you can skim everything rather than getting really into it. I lost interest after a while. Interesting concept, but personally I didn't really connect with the characters and felt they were a bit too cliched. Despite not enjoying it that much, I would still recommend playing it.

I bought this game in hope of having something to stream. The gameplay looked great so I couldn't wait to get it however 3 hours in and it was all over. The game feels half finished, like the developers got a writers block halfway through the story and hurried to finish it. 

There's only one story so no other challenges or modes to play.

[h1]Thoughts[/h1]

So let start off with saying I purchased the full game after playing the demo, looking back the demo actually offers everything that you would find in the main game so I would highly suggest playing the demo before making a purchase and understand that the gameplay isnt any different.

The premise of the game is to locate pertinent information about certain suspects in response to a terror attack, the information is uploaded to a system for your superior to review. The superior talks to pretty much every time you upload something, questioning the information and how it can be used against them.  The communication is totally one way and unfortunately because of the limited information you can upload sometimes it is taken very much out of context. e.g. someone was torturing someone else with muffins…. Uploading this to the system and the superior freaked out saying this person needs investigating because they like to torture people.  Hmm, I get that is the game design but yeah it’s a bit bizarre.

I use the term locate here very loosely because the game essentially spoon feeds you documents, links and webpages that contains the important information, the task at hand is to determine if the information is actually useful or not.  Every now and then you get some information which conflicts and you have to upload just one piece of information however this type of interaction doesn’t happen that often which is a shame.

I also didn’t like how the story abruptly ended, it wasn’t obvious in any way that if I upload this bit of information the game would finish.  I was taken completely by surprise and I understand there are multiple endings available but the choice just wasn’t obvious.

Despite playing the demo I still assumed the game would offer a lot more detective work later on, I assumed that I would need to locate web pages, search people and scan the documents but no.  The system finds everything and then sends you it gift tied in a little star shaped parcel.  All you do is drag and drop blue text to the box on the left and occasionally choose between one bit of yellow text and another bit of yellow text.

Overall I think this game offers great potential but it falls down with its boring repetitive gameplay that require zero thought or analysis.  If you are wanting a detective text based game look at Hacknet, for me that that is far superior to this as its on you to find and locate the information rather than it being spoon fed to you.

With only 2 hours of massively immersive gameplay, Orwell offers a trully Orwell-like peek on what is it like to play the Big Brother, with all its perks and consequences. Albeit playing out in only the same, social media-like screen, this game doesn't need more to have a huge effect on the player. With its carefully thought out plots, we feel the weight of every decision we make, and we feel lives hanging on a thin thread that we spin. I developed a deep connection to each of the characters, and even if they were indeed guilty, the feeling that I have to be the one to condemn them is a very unsettling one - and this is what Orwell does best. Not many things can show what comes with power in such a strong and sincere way. Highly recommended!

I'm only partway through, but so far i've found the game to be very interesting but the mechanics to be somewhat annoying.  The game has an interesting premise, almost reminiscient of papers please but with a polygon theme instead of pixels.  You read a large amount of data and choose what from the highlighted options to feed to a detective working the case.  But sometimes the foreshadowing in the data is obvious and you really want to communicate some of the non-highlighted data.  Sometimes you read one item, you think you found an important point of data (which is colored yellow, but you're not really looking for that, you're reading the interesting story), and then two pages later you find more appropriate data that conflicts with what you sent, but you can't edit what you've already sent so the detective can't get the right info.  I find that particular mechanic very odd.  Overall i enjoy the game, but it's a little frustrating to play.  The story is highly engrossing but i'm going to have to start over and be more careful about what i send.

An interesting puzzle/story game with a heavy-handed message.

Gameplay revolves around using a web-browser-like interface to look for information on persons of interest.  The interface is completely adequate for that purpose and that's about all you can say about the mechanics of the game.  

I'm not sure that the game has a Lose-State so you're essentially free to do whatever you want which is cool.  Personally, I'd have liked a few more red herrings or maybe a thing where my handler buddy gets weirded out while I obsessively upload as many pictures of everyone that I could find.  Also, I enjoyed the time limit aspect of one part of the game and seeing that in other places would have been cool.

The story and writing do all the heavy lifting for the game and I feel like it did a good job.  The scenario is fairly realistic and the characters are written well enough that you can get a feel for what's going on without things feeling too obvious, contrived, or arbitrary... except for one thing: there is an ending that (as far as I can tell) is entirely missing from the game and it feels like a missed opportunity to not allow players to pursue it.  I'm sure it's entirely intentional but I disagree with it.

Anyhow, the game's got 5 episodes and each of those take about an hour to complete.  I'd say it's well worth it if you can pick it up for 10bux or less.

I did not think I would like Orwell but I do. The user environment is believable and using hyperlinked content to build a profile of your suspect is a good way to conceal the linear nature of the game. I haven't played too far yet, but suspect the overarching social justice themes will result in a fairly hamfisted ending. Still, I'm having fun playing this. Thus I recommend it.

In general there need to be more well-written visual novel and CYOA type adventure games for adults. Orwell falls under that category, IMO. It'd be interesting to see more games in that vein which don't overtly reach for social significance, and allow themselves to be compelling hypernarratives without trying to morally educate the player.

[h1] THE GAME THAT WILL LEAVE YOU EMOTIONALLY CRIPPLED [/h1]

TL;DR Worth the price of $10 USD, incredible story. You're gonna like the way you get hooked. I guarantee it.

*sigh* This game is gonna leave me scarred for a little bit.

So. Orwell is a short interactive narrative game where you take the seat behind a new, high tech computer system called "Orwell." This system is meant to be a means to an end, a platform for an investigative war or terrorism.

The story is deep and rich. And there's a lot of different events going on, all of which tie into the decisions you make and how the characters feel about everything going on.

It all starts off with a single bombing and a letter. At first, all seems simple. You watch a little CCTV footie, you think "OH THAT'S THE PERSON. RIGHT THERE. THIS GAME'S GONNA BE EASY AF." No. Because soon, you don't know what to think. You'll find yourself conflicted as the information provided to you begins to conflict. You begin to feel lost, like you're not really sure what or who you are looking for.

At the end. It'll take you for a loop. And you're given a huge decision. A decision that impacts who you are.

[b] Do you go through with it? Make it all finally end? [i] Or do you sympathize? Bring everyting to a fitting end? [/i] [/b]

It all comes down to what you feel justice is for you. In fact, this game will have you questioning that the entire time.


Now, I'd like to bring up something I felt was... ehhhhhh, displeasing. We'll go with displeasing.

[h1] THIS GAME IS RATHER SHORT [/h1]

Or so it seems. 

There are a lot of things to consider. If you just focus on the main issues, the main information, yes. It can seem a little short lived. But if you take the time to read everything, get to know the characters for who they are, their interests, their emotions, their... [i]thoughts[/i]... It's really not that short at all. And all of this information can affect your ability to make decisions in this game. At times, you'll feel something is unjust, or unfounded. You'll struggle at times to think about what information is relevant.

I've said it before. I'll say it again. [b] The way you play this game is heavily reliant on your own sense of justice. [/b]

So think about it. And think about it again.

What decisions will you make?

This game had me on the edge of my seat through the whole experience. 

One of my favourite games by far.

I started out thinking this was gonna be a decent experience, finding out info on people using Orwellian tactics, and that's about it. I was kinda wrong. You don't have access to everything from the get-go. People start to cover their traces when they're up to no good.

You are a contractor for Orwell, a government surveillance agency as an outside contractor. Yoor focus is to find evidence against a terrorist group and make sure they can no longer bomb people and places. You extract data from a variety of sources, articles, private messages between users (You need to find out their phone numbers/emails yourself) and access thier personal devices (You'll need a device ID for that though, which may or may not be hard to find). You tap phone calls and messages to learn about each character and their role in the story, and you can decide their fates.

Here's the catch: your superiors can only see what you upload to them. You decide what they can and can't see.

The first episode is more of a tutorial than anything, then episode 2 serves as an intro, and 3, 4, and 5 is where the story really takes off. The finale left me blown away, and I am definitely looking foward to the next game by these developers.

If you want a great short story for a lazy day (or lazy days), check this out.

This game is interesting.

I must preface this with saying that there is very little gameplay - the gameplay mostly consists of going through files and websites and dragging content - and a playthrough of the game takes around 5 hours (took me 4.4 hours but I did my playthrough over one day).

Despite the little actual gameplay involved, Orwell isn't dull whatsoever. The little control you have makes you feel like a detective while simultaneously making you question the morality of your actions. 

Without spoiling too much, this game has some intense and surprising moments, created by great visual and audial nuances. It is reminiscent of a thriller in this particular sense, hence the developers naming the genre of Orwell a 'Privacy Invasion Thriller'.

Orwell is a thought-provoking, story-rich, creative and incredibly immersive game. I'd highly recommend this to anyone who likes interactive story-telling games (especially those set in a dystopian world), or anyone who likes detective work.


[b] Criticism [/b]

[list]
[*]I would have really loved to have seen some voice work in the game, there is none at all.
[*]I would like the experience to be longer, however this isn't too much of an issue.
[*]I also would have liked to see a bit more features in the game, however, what it does, it does well.
[/list]

Overall Rating: 7.8/10

Well, it was everuthing I expected. Ever read 1984? Watched the series Person of interest? Ever wondered how privacy and safety are balancing in this world? Ever wondered how powerfull information can be? Not easily creeped out by knowledge yourself? Then, this is a game for you.

You play an investigator working for a government "Big Brother" agency, named Orwell. As an objective observer you review evidence that your advisor sends your way, and respond to it by uploading what you consider to be relevant details regarding potential suspects in a crime - a crime that ends up only being an element of the overall story. 

The story itself feels well thought out, although some of the literal interpretations of your data by your advisor are jarring - context really is everything and some information is easily misunderstood by those you work under. I found some of these limitations to be irksome - if I was doing this sort of job in real life I would certainly have included some of the information your superiors reject because it provides a more rounded view of the suspects.

The most negative thing I would say about my experience with Orwell overall is that some of the consequences to choices felt contrived, forcing you off-track in a way that was obviously a narrative techinique. 

Entertaining, could have been longer but for the price it worked out to be reasonable. Shame it's a single story really, the setting had a lot of scope for expansion. The game does offer some replay value though. 

Essentially a choice-and-consequence game with an element of mystery.

What I like about the game was that I went into the game trying my best to do right within the constraints of a flawed system, and...well, let's just say the road to hell is paved with good intentions. So, yes, the gameplay can be annoyingly restrictive - you won't get to make choices that you want to make sometimes - but it makes sense, given the premise.

Very smart point and click game with a great narative. If you enjoy a slower paced game that you can sink yourself into with a rediculous time burden, this is a game for you. i tend to prefer survival games and action rpg's, but this is definitely keeping me glued to my screen.

I'm speechless as in what to say for this game, since the entire story totally got me so hard that I'm quite sad it's >only< 5 hours long.

I had quite high expectations, considering the price of the game and the game's length, and I'm very happy to say that Orwell didn't disappoint, not even a little. Episode 1, which is also included in the demo is very short and serves more like a "tutorial" than actual gameplay, and after completing it I was afraid that the rest would look similar - nothing like that, all other 4 episodes were so intense and well-written that I immediately went back to my previous happy state and enjoyed my fun.

And believe me - I hate all sort of VNs and games with huge amount of text, they're usually boring for me and I quickly lose my interest, that's why I was a bit sceptical at first whether I'm going to enjoy Orwell, but I decided to go with it due to a nice -43% (bundle) discount, and I can say that the experience is well worth the money, even at full price.

You should DEFINITELY grab the game if you're interested in all sort of government spying on people, but apart from that it'd be also interesting position for people interested in "working" for government in general, doing detective work, connecting various pieces together and enjoying awesome story. In fact, the story is the most polished thing in the entire game, and it's alone worth the time and money spent on the title, that's why I'd recommend this title even for people that expect more gameplay than reading, such as myself.

From the bad things, the game can seem a bit too "casual", especially for more oldschool gamers like myself - I'd appreciate difficulty setting that would turn off highlighting relevant facts, and definitely allow to jump onto conclusions with only half-available data. Don't get me wrong - the game is awesome and those are not any crucial things that would heavily affect the gameplay, but I kinda miss the option of actually "losing", by jumping onto false assumption and getting fired. Losing should definitely be an option here.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time, this is at least a 9/10 from me - missing point only for being too casual, although that didn't stop me from enjoying the awesome story that the devs coded for me, since I had a lot of fun. I can definitely recommend the title to everyone!

Now this is a thriller. I love how this game manages to walk the knife's edge between tense mystery and ethical conundrums.

It's a very detective-y, snooping sort of game. You're ferreting out clues in blog posts and text chats and more, trying to stop terrible crimes from happening. That means there's a lot of reading, of course, and it's to Orwell's credit that most of it still feels fascinating through several hours of play. I was committed to solving the mystery, but as I delved deeper into the story, I felt increasingly ambivalent about my role in the narrative: I HAD to snoop to save lives, but each piece of information I deemed relevant might result in an endangered or wrongly imprisoned suspect. You're voiceless, unable to shout "STOP I'm not SURE this seems more nuanced than that." Your only power lies in the information you pass along, 

All in all, I really enjoyed this game, and I'll definitely replay it. While I found several of Orwell's mysteries, I know there's more to uncover.

Orwell can best be described as a chilling depiction of just how intrusive surveillance can be on ordinary people's lives. You play as an outsourced investigator working for "The Nation" with the goal of finding out the truth behind a terrorist attack. This is done by recording the actions of people via the surveillance tool 'Orwell, which can monitor phone conversations, internet usage and other methods of communication, all of which we take for granted in our society. 

While the game is relatively short (it only took me about 4 hours to complete a run of the story), the plot is both entertaining and unnerving, acting as a commentary of what we know various governments throughout the Western world are doing. According to Orwell, everyone is guilty until proven innocent, and even then the innocent can be caught in the crossfire. 

I wouldn't say it's the most fun I've had with a game, much like Spec Ops: The Line it's more about the message it is trying to convey, which it does flawlessly.

Be prepared to read a lot, because reading is essentially what the game is about. If you [i]are[/i] prepared, the game will reward you.

Orwell is essentially a story told with some interactive elements. While there are choices to make throughout, the overall story arch seems fairly linear. This is not negative though. The game has a nice pace, well-written dialogue, and interesting twists.

The game is not perfect though. For example, it seemed like I was supposed to feel bad about what I was doing, but the game didn't [i]really[/i] manage to make me feel this way, even though I am quite privacy-concerned myself. This is probably due to the fact that the game does not fully immerse the player (at least not for me).

Nevertheless, I highly recommend the game for its story-telling. The subject matter is important, and I'm happy when games try to convey an important message.

(the Steam screenshots showing a 3D environment are a bit misleading. These are from the intro, and the game is entirely made up reading different material).

Do you think information is neutral? Better think again.
Orwell put you in the shoes of a crowd sourced Big Brother (or a sort of NSA agent) and with a compelling narrative shows you that, even if you have nothing to hide, your info is precious nonetheless.

While the central themes and the nods to Nineteen Eighty-Four can get a little heavy-handed at times, this is generally a very intriguing, effectively exciting bit of narrative-driven gaming, ideal for anyone with an interest in the theme of governmental control and online privacy.

Orwell is a strange mix of Papers Please, Her Story, and visual novels. A very well-written, engaging storyline told through interacting with a limited surveillance interface. The characters are very interesting, though I do think some twists are for twisting's sake.

Still, I recommend it as an experiment, especially as a way to get through the narrative in the game.  Dialog seems natural and not too expositional.

If you like stories about complex relationships and social networks, this might be for you.

Fantastic game. Immersive, intriguing, great idea from the origin. I've always love playing a game like these and it's such a niche thing to find: to play as someone using a computer to investigate and analyze. The closest I've come to is Her Story (another story rich game, really great if you've got the time and your into that sort of thing). 

I think one of Orwell's best features is the how your decisions can effect the outcome of the game. It also tests your morality and your own ethics. It may start a conversation in you about the far reaching power technology has to achieve absolute security measures. Is it right in order to save people from getting killed? Or should privacy be preserved in order to prevent non-criminals from being lumped as potential suspects? Overall, it will make you think afterwards about what you think is wrong or right. 


Don't play Orwell if you're in a rush; it's more a game you play when you got a few hours and have a cup of coffee next to you. You will be faced with conflicting evidence and be forced to use your judgement. This a great story driven game with really cool art style, neat interface, and a story line that makes me second-guess whose side you're really on.

ohh this is really, really well-done. To a large extent, this is what I've always wanted from a mystery game: being able to/having to think and reason for yourself, draw conclusions, then have them reflect in the game - rather than being taken through a sequence of 'revelations' by the game plot. Partially reminds me of old-school RPGs that didn't write down all the relevant information in the quest log for you and/or spell out the revelations and point you in the right direction - you had to put two and two together yourself. I actually took notes playing this game!

Things that made it a good mystery-like experience: Having to make judgement calls based on incomplete information. Occasional moments of adrenaline rush as you make genuinely (as far as I can tell as a player, anyway) time-sensitive calls. Real consequences that you can retroactively attribute to your actions (and adjust your strategy).

Story and gameplay integrate together very neatly. The Datachunk mechanic feels a bit hokey at first, until you realize that the system really does require your human judgement, and research beyond the highlighted datachunks, to work well.

Technically, this game is probably very easy to "complete", but I don't know if I would call any completion "beating" it.  I really felt clever when I figured out (part of) the mystery myself, and that actually affected the outcome.

Could probably write a whole paper on this game and questions like "what is winning/losing in a game?" "what is or is not gameplay?" "who is a villain and who is a hero?"  if one were inclined to write papers about new-media-like subjects.
I do agree the game is simple and quick, but still very entertaining.  I thought it was unique and really hope to see similar games.

I expected to have to do more "detective work", but this is just a choices-don't-make-sense-but-they-matter experience.  Especially in the final chapter, I had little clue what I was supposed to accomplish, and then suddenly I accomplished something and the game was over.

If I could give this a Thumbs-Sideways, I would.  There are a few interesting "scenes" and moments that were surprising, but as it stands, I didn't feel like I was enjoying myself.  Just uploading "datachunks" and waiting for the game to find more datachunks to be uploaded.  Occasionally I had to decide between two conflicting pieces of data, but those choices were less-than-half of the game.  Maybe one-third of the game is "decisions" like that, and the rest is just dragging datachunks from one side of the screen to the other.  Or in some cases, deciding NOT to drag a datachunk from one side of the screen to the other, because it might be misunderstood by your superiors. For example, one comment on a website in-game says "oh no! the torture! ;)" in a playful manner about being bribed with muffins, but if you upload it your boss takes it to mean LITERAL TORTURE and freaks out about it.  So you're told to upload "all the relevant data" but then have no say in how it gets interpreted or used, which impacts upon the relevance of said data.

If you like games that try to make political-statements about things, this is probably up your alley.  I just wanted to solve puzzles, connect clues, etc.  The game highlights all the relevant information, and then connects it to things for you.  Not TERRIBLE, but not what I expected or hoped for. :(
